name: Timeouts
explanation: Users need to be warned in advance about how long they have before inactivity could cause them to lose their data, unless that data is actually kept safe for more than 20 hours of inactivity before anything is lost. This is broader than session-login timeouts alone; it covers any situation where simply not acting for a while could wipe out entered data, like an abandoned shopping cart or a partially filled survey that clears itself after a period of inactivity.
whoItAffects: People who need to step away mid-task, whether due to a disability that requires rest breaks, a distraction, or simply needing time to think something through, are at risk of losing their work if they don't know a countdown to data loss exists. Being told upfront how much inactive time is allowed lets someone plan around it, save their progress manually, or come back within the window, rather than discovering the loss only after it has already happened.

codeExample.bad:
<!-- No indication anywhere that inactivity will clear the form -->
<form id="survey-form">
  <label for="feedback">Your feedback</label>
  <textarea id="feedback" name="feedback"></textarea>
</form>
<!-- The form silently resets after 30 minutes of inactivity -->
codeExample.good: Your progress is saved automatically, but will be cleared after 30 minutes of inactivity. Submit or save a draft before then.

howToTest: Look for any place where leaving a form or task idle for a while could cause data loss: an abandoned cart, an auto-clearing draft, a session that logs out silently. Check whether the page discloses, before you'd lose anything, how long you have before that happens. If there's no such warning anywhere in the interface or its instructions, check whether the data is instead preserved for at least 20 hours of inactivity; if neither is true, this fails.

check.question: An online form auto-clears any unsaved entries after 15 minutes of inactivity, but the page never mentions this time limit anywhere, and the data isn't preserved beyond that point. Does this pass SC 2.2.6 Timeouts?
choices: Yes, because 15 minutes is a common and reasonable timeout duration
No, because the user is never warned of the inactivity duration that causes data loss, and the data isn't preserved for 20+ hours
Yes, because auto-clearing forms is a well-known web convention users should expect
It depends only on whether the form has fewer than five fields
